text:
The debate surrounding #Starlink in #India is not really about internet speeds, rural connectivity or even Elon Musk.

It is about #sovereignty 
History teaches us that nations rarely lose strategic autonomy overnight. More often, dependence develops gradually through systems, networks and institutions that become too important to function without.

The #BritishEastIndiaCompany did not arrive in India as a conquering army. It arrived as a commercial enterprise promising trade, access to global markets and economic opportunity. Over time, commercial influence evolved into political leverage, strategic control and eventually colonial rule.

The world of the 21st century is different, but the underlying principle remains relevant.

Today, influence is exercised not only through territory and military power but through data, communications infrastructure, digital platforms, satellite networks and technological dependence.

This is where Starlink becomes a strategic question rather than merely a telecommunications project.

Supporters correctly point out that satellite internet can transform connectivity in remote regions, improve disaster response and bridge digital divides. These are real benefits.

However, strategic planners must also ask a different set of questions:
“Who controls the network?
Who ultimately decides where service is available?”

What happens during a geopolitical crisis?
Can a sovereign nation guarantee uninterrupted access if the infrastructure is owned, operated and controlled by a foreign private entity?

The Ukraine conflict offers a powerful example.
Reports revealed that Starlink services were restricted during a planned Ukrainian operation targeting Russian naval assets near Crimea. The result was that the operation could not proceed as intended because the communications network required for execution was unavailable.

Regardless of one’s views on the decision, the larger geopolitical lesson is clear:
A private company and its leadership possessed the ability to influence the operational options available to a sovereign state during an active conflict.

That reality should concern every serious strategic planner in the world.
The issue is not whether Elon Musk was right or wrong.

The issue is whether any nation should place critical national communications infrastructure in a position where ultimate operational control rests outside its sovereign authority.

For India, this question carries even greater significance.

India faces an increasingly contested security environment stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. #Communications resilience is not merely an economic requirement; it is a #nationalsecurity necessity.

This does not mean rejecting foreign technology.
India has benefited enormously from international investment, technology partnerships and global integration.

But integration should never become dependence.
The ideal outcome is not isolation but strategic balance: encouraging innovation while ensuring robust regulatory oversight, #dataprotection, local compliance requirements and #sovereigncontrol mechanisms.

The lesson of the #EastIndiaCompany is often misunderstood.
The danger was never trade itself.

The danger was allowing critical leverage to accumulate outside Indian control.

As technology becomes the new arena of geopolitical competition, nations must remember a simple principle:
Infrastructure creates dependence.
Dependence creates leverage.
Leverage creates influence.

And influence, if left unchecked, can eventually challenge sovereignty itself.

India was colonised once through commerce and influence.
The next challenge, if it ever comes, will not arrive on sailing ships.

It will arrive through networks, platforms, satellites and systems that become too important to question

That is why the Starlink debate is not merely abt connectivity.
It is about ensuring that 🇮🇳’s digital future remains firmly under Indian sovereign control #JaiHind

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

text:
How to Read Iran's 26-Page Midterm Letter to American Voters in 10 Minutes

Iran picked a side in November. The same regime that named America the Great Satan spent 26 pages asking you to change who runs Congress, and it did not pick Republicans.

On Tuesday, September 29, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps published "An Open Letter to the Honorable People of the United States of America." Twenty-five pages or twenty-six, depending on who did the counting. Either way, that is longer than most of my students' research papers. And better formatted, frankly, which hurts.

The IRGC, for anyone keeping score at home, is the outfit President Trump designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2019. It is now giving civics lessons to Ohio.

What is next, a terrorist army writing campaign literature for an American election... oh. Wait. I was just handed a note. They already did that.

I teach science, so we will do this the way I grade a lab report. Claim. Evidence. Conclusion. But first I owe you something, because I cannot read this letter the way a pundit reads it. I read it as a man Iran has already tried to kill.

— WHY THIS ONE IS PERSONAL —

I was an Army medic in Iraq.

Iran's militias blew up my vehicle while I was sitting in it. And they hurt my gunner.

I am going to say that again, slower, because I need the IRGC's English-language PR department to understand it. They. Hurt. My. Gunner.

If you have never ridden in a turret-topped truck, here is what you need to know. The gunner is the one standing up. Half of his body is out in the open so the rest of us can sit down behind armor. He is the first set of eyes, the first one exposed, and when something goes wrong he is the first one it finds. Every medic in every convoy knows exactly where his gunner is at every second. You do not lose track of your gunner. Ever.

So when I hear a regime spokesman say there is not "a single verifiable instance" of the IRGC hurting anyone, I do not need a fact-checker. I need a minute. And maybe a walk around the block.

The State Department has stated that Iran was responsible for the deaths of at least 603 American service members in Iraq between 2003 and 2011, mostly through militias it trained, funded, and handed explosively formed penetrators. An EFP is a copper plate that turns into a molten slug and punches through armor like it is wet cardboard. I know what one does to a truck. I know what it does to the men inside. I did not learn it from a documentary.

And now that same regime wants to tell me how to vote.

No one hurts my gunner. Nobody. And they sure as heck do not get a vote in my country afterward.

— WHAT THE LETTER ACTUALLY SAYS —

Alright. Deep breath. Back to the lab report.

To be fair, and I am always fair, the letter never prints the letter D. It does not have to.

It tells Americans that politicians win votes through "deception and false promises, as Trump did," and that we can "change the makeup of the government" by choosing differently. It calls the President a tyrant. It claims Iran won the war. (Bold strategy, considering the last seven months.) It wants American support for Israel ended and our overseas bases closed. Then it offers "peaceful coexistence."

And then, in the same document, it warns that people around the world will set fire to American interests and assets if we do not change course.

Coexistence. With a lit match in the other hand. It reads less like a peace offer and more like a breakup text from a stalker. "I just want what's best for you. Also, I know where you park."

Now, the part that matters for your ballot. President Trump is not on it this November. The only way to "change the makeup of the government" in 2026 is to change who controls the House and the Senate. There are two parties on that ballot.

The IRGC can count to two. So can you.

Jonathan Turley put it about as well as anyone could: it is not a good sign when the IRGC shifts from "Death to America" to "Vote Democratic."

— "WHY IS NOBODY REPORTING THIS?" —

Precision matters in this classroom, so here it is. Some outlets did. Reuters ran it. The New York Post ran it. The State Department answered it on Wednesday and called it a desperate smokescreen.

So let me ask the better question. How many minutes did your favorite evening newscast give it?

A designated terrorist organization publicly asking Americans to remove one party from power, five weeks before a federal election. If the Kremlin had mailed voters a 26-page letter begging them to vote Republican, we would know the font. We would know the paper weight. Rachel Maddow would have a corkboard and red string by Thursday.

Quinn's Law Number 2: If you want to know what liberals are up to, pay attention to what they accuse conservatives of doing. We spent years being told that a foreign power picking a side in an American election was a five-alarm emergency. It still is. It just gets a lot less interesting when the foreign power picks the "right" side.

— THIS IS NOT IRAN'S FIRST ELECTION —

The letter is new. The strategy is not.

o August 2020: the National Intelligence Council assessed that Iran was running an influence campaign to undermine the President and divide the country, and that Khamenei probably authorized it.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

Burlington vape shop bars unaccompanied women after owner charged with sexual assault: @ScarlettGrace92 

The sex-based policy appeared after the owner of Vape on Plains was charged with sexually assaulting a woman who police say was alone with him at a store location.

A Burlington vape shop barred unaccompanied women from entering the store after its owner was charged with sexually assaulting a woman at one of his store locations.

A notice posted at one of the Vape on Plains locations told customers that, “due to an ongoing situation,” female customers who arrived alone could not be served inside.

Instead, women were instructed to knock on a window where a catalogue of prices and flavours had been provided. Male customers were still permitted inside.

The policy followed the September 8 arrest of 64-year-old Burlington resident Mouhamad “Frank” Sabra, owner of Vape on Plains and Vape on Plains II.

@HaltonPolice allege an adult woman was sexually assaulted after attending the Vape on Plains II location on Plains Road East while she was alone in the store with Sabra.

Sabra was charged with sexual assault and failing to comply with a probation order. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Police also released Sabra’s photograph, saying investigators believe there may be additional victims and asking anyone with information or a similar experience at either store to come forward.

The Plains Road West business had previously run afoul of provincial vaping regulations.

Halton Public Health records show that in March 2023, the business, then listed as “Vape On Plains And Gift Garage,” was convicted of selling a vapour product to someone under 19 and received a $400 set fine.

In May 2026, it was convicted again, this time for offering to sell an improperly packaged vapour product, and fined $365.

Then came a very different controversy. Following the allegation against the owner, it was female customers who found themselves on the other side of the door.

Section 1 of Ontario’s Human Rights Code guarantees equal treatment with respect to services, goods and facilities without discrimination because of sex, raising questions about the legality of treating customers differently based on whether they are male or female.

The notice quickly went viral, with some social media users characterizing the policy as “Sharia law” and even referring to the country as the “Islamic Republic of Canada.”

A subsequent video posted online showed the notice had been removed.

Police have not disclosed the date of the alleged assault or publicly confirmed whether additional alleged victims have since come forward. Their investigation remains ongoing.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
DISTRICT OF MINNESOTA

THOMAS EVENSTAD,
Plaintiff,

v.

CITY OF MINNEAPOLIS; JACOB FREY; TODDRICK BARNETTE; MINNEAPOLIS POLICE DEPARTMENT; HENNEPIN COUNTY; MARY MORIARTY; LES HARRIS; and DOES 1–20,

Defendants.

Case No. _____________

COMPLAINT

Plaintiff Thomas Evenstad, appearing pro se, alleges:

This case arises from a violent attack against Plaintiff during a political event in Minneapolis on or about August 22, 2026.

Plaintiff was present as an unarmed political participant and was wearing an “EVENSTAD FOR GOVERNOR” hat.

Before the attack, Plaintiff was positioned near a windowsill that provided him with a safer elevated position from which to observe the event.

Plaintiff had occupied that same or similar position during the January 2026 event involving Jake Lang.

An MPD officer ordered Plaintiff to leave the windowsill.

Plaintiff complied with the officer's order and left the position where he believed he was comparatively safe.

Plaintiff alleges that MPD personnel were actively monitoring the area. Plaintiff observed MPD personnel from an elevated position using binoculars while Plaintiff was wearing his “EVENSTAD FOR GOVERNOR” hat.

After Plaintiff was ordered away from the windowsill, people in the surrounding crowd began directing hostile political insults toward him, including calling him a “Trumper running for Governor,” “pedo,” and “rapist.”

Plaintiff was then mobbed and surrounded.

Plaintiff was unarmed and did not pose a threat to the crowd.

Plaintiff was punched and kicked, his hair was pulled, his political hat was ripped from his head, and he was knocked to the ground.

Plaintiff alleges that members of the crowd attempted to take his property and stomped or attempted to stomp him while he was down.

Plaintiff was eventually helped back to his feet.

Plaintiff attempted to evacuate the area and reach safety.

Plaintiff alleges that members of the crowd followed him as he attempted to escape.

Defendant Les Harris approached Plaintiff from behind.

Plaintiff alleges that Harris filmed himself approaching Plaintiff and then sprayed chemical irritant directly into Plaintiff's face from less than approximately three feet away.

The chemical irritant entered Plaintiff's eyes and immediately caused severe pain and loss of vision.

Plaintiff fell to the ground again.

Plaintiff alleges that Harris's own recording documents the incident and that Harris subsequently posted the recording on Instagram.

Plaintiff eventually called 911.

As some vision began to return, Plaintiff remained in severe pain and had extremely blurred vision.

Approximately 10–20 MPD officers established a protective cordon around Plaintiff while he waited for emergency medical assistance.

Plaintiff was transported to an emergency department.

Plaintiff alleges that he was treated for chemical burns and severe facial and eye exposure.

Plaintiff's vision remained severely blurred for more than 48 hours.

Plaintiff experienced substantial eye pain for several days before his vision and pain eventually improved.

The incident caused Plaintiff substantial physical pain, emotional distress, fear, humiliation, and trauma.

Plaintiff subsequently provided MPD with Harris's alleged recording of the attack.

Plaintiff also provided information and evidence concerning the attack to the Hennepin County Attorney's Office.

Plaintiff alleges that, despite providing this evidence, no arrest or criminal charge has been communicated to him concerning Harris's alleged attack.

Plaintiff is not asking this Court to order a criminal prosecution. Plaintiff seeks civil relief for governmental conduct and for the injuries caused by the assault.

Plaintiff seeks discovery concerning how MPD received, preserved, investigated, and handled his complaint and evidence.

Plaintiff also seeks discovery concerning communications between MPD and the Hennepin County Attorney's Office concerning Plaintiff's complaint.

Plaintiff alleges that the City had advance knowledge of the August event and had an opportunity to evaluate public-safety risks.

The January 2026 event involving Jake Lang is relevant because Plaintiff personally witnessed serious crowd violence surrounding that event.

During the January event, Plaintiff alleges that he helped Jake Lang escape through a parking garage because Plaintiff believed Lang was in danger.

Plaintiff alleges that the January event was sufficiently dangerous that it should have been considered when planning security for another Lang-related event.

Plaintiff does not allege that Lang's political beliefs, by themselves, justified excluding him from the August event.

Plaintiff alleges instead that the City and MPD had an obligation to plan for known safety risks in a viewpoint-neutral manner.

Plaintiff also alleges that he had previously been subjected to substantial governmental restrictions, including exclusion from three metropolitan-area counties for five years and GPS monitoring for five years.

Plaintiff does not claim that Lang was legally required to receive the same restrictions.

Plaintiff alleges that the difference is relevant to whether governmental authorities applied public-safety standards consistently and without political or viewpoint discrimination.

Defendant Toddrick Barnette was Minneapolis Commissioner of Community Safety during the relevant period.

Plaintiff does not presently know the full extent of Barnette's involvement in planning, supervising, coordinating, or reviewing the August event.

Defendant Jacob Frey was Mayor of Minneapolis during the relevant period.

Plaintiff seeks discovery concerning any municipal policies, directives, public-safety decisions, or policymaking actions attributable to the Mayor that caused or contributed to Plaintiff's injuries.

Plaintiff does not allege that Frey personally assaulted Plaintiff.

Any individual-capacity claim against Frey is based upon facts that may be established through discovery concerning his personal involvement.

Defendant Mary Moriarty was Hennepin County Attorney during the relevant period.

Plaintiff alleges that the Hennepin County Attorney's Office received evidence concerning his assault.

Plaintiff seeks discovery concerning the handling of that evidence and the communications between the County Attorney's Office and MPD.

Plaintiff recognizes that prosecutorial immunity may apply to protected prosecutorial acts.

Plaintiff therefore seeks to hold Moriarty individually liable only to the extent discovery establishes actionable conduct outside any protected prosecutorial function.

Plaintiff further alleges that another person, known publicly as Zak X, was harassed and threatened during or surrounding the same general event.

Plaintiff alleges that some of the same individuals involved in conduct directed at Plaintiff were involved in conduct directed at Zak X.

Plaintiff seeks discovery concerning complaints and police responses involving other persons who may have experienced similar conduct.

Plaintiff alleges that the circumstances raise serious questions concerning whether the City and its police department adequately protected persons engaged in political activity from foreseeable violence.

Plaintiff further alleges that governmental action affecting him must be examined to determine whether his political expression or candidacy played a role in the treatment he received.

42 U.S.C. § 1983 — FIRST AMENDMENT

Plaintiff incorporates paragraphs 1–60.

Plaintiff was engaged in protected political expression.

Plaintiff was openly identifying himself as a political candidate by wearing an “EVENSTAD FOR GOVERNOR” hat.

Plaintiff alleges that he was subjected to adverse governmental treatment in circumstances involving hostility toward his political identity and expression.

Plaintiff seeks damages and other appropriate relief to the extent discovery establishes that a government defendant retaliated against Plaintiff or otherwise violated his First Amendment rights.

COUNT II
42 U.S.C. § 1983 — FOURTEENTH AMENDMENT

Plaintiff incorporates paragraphs 1–65.

Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.
